author: reek
body: codex/os/kernel/IdentityManager.codex is cited by exactly one chapter (apps/works/FirstBoot) and no battery compiled either, so it sat broken, then merely compiling, and nothing ever executed a line of it. This is the chapter behind CurrentPlan gap 2.

author: reek
body: The ceremony as a whole is not deterministic -- idm-collect-keyboard-entropy mixes get-ticks into the seed -- but its cryptography is: every function below is a pure function of its arguments, and the entropy only decides what arguments they get. So the crypto is testable today, and it is the half that was wrong.

author: reek
body: Nothing could see it, and this is why the test asserts a LENGTH and a zero-count rather than an encrypt/decrypt round trip. The same wrong key was used to encrypt at first boot and to decrypt at unlock, so the ceremony round-tripped perfectly: the passphrase worked, the key loaded, and the only symptom was a number nobody read. A round trip agrees with itself. Ask a question it cannot answer by agreeing.

author: reek
body: A 32-byte key, not 128. The buggy form answered 128.

author: reek
body: Changing the salt must change the key. A derivation that ignored an argument would pass both tests above.

author: reek
body: idm-generate-keypair is a pure function of its seed: it takes 32 bytes and asks Ed25519 for the public key. Same seed, same keypair -- and a different seed had better not give the same one.

author: reek
body: idm-take-bytes pads a short source with zeros rather than truncating to what it has -- the property first-boot relies on when the hash is shorter than the key.

author: reek
body: idm-bytes-eq is the passphrase comparison. It must not call unequal lengths equal, and it must not call a prefix a match.

author: reek
body: idm-zero-list wipes the plaintext buffers on every path out of unlock. It must actually zero them.
